Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 10 watermarking schemes, 5 model scales, multiple text lengths, with thorough ablation studies

Circular approximation of watermark distribution P_wm: uses paraphrasing prompts to approximate what paraphrasing should evade; approximation quality not analyzed
Lack of theoretical justification for why semantic preservation and KL divergence objectives should align; connection between theory (KL) and practice (P-SP) underdeveloped

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 10 watermarking schemes, multiple model sizes, and long-form text (1500 tokens), revealing systematic vulnerabilities
Addresses an important problem of rigorously evaluating watermark robustness under adaptive attacks, moving beyond average-case to worst-case analysis
Strong practical results: 98.5% ESR on Unigram with only 100 training samples, significantly outperforming GPT-4o
Interesting empirical findings about system prompts, reasoning capability, and test-time scaling effects on watermark removal
Adaptive robustness radius provides a principled metric inspired by certified robustness; Theorem 1 offers concrete KL-based lower bounds with clear interpretation
Excellent generalization to OOD data and robustness to mixed-key training with minimal performance degradation
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: RLCracker is primarily GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) applied to watermark removal; core RL method is not novel
Weak connection between theory and practice: adaptive robustness radius is never empirically validated or directly used; no test of whether computed r_KL predicts actual attack success

Critical unvalidated assumptions: Sub-Gaussian detector score assumption (Assumption 1) is essential for Theorem 1 but lacks empirical validation; distribution approximations (Ph via πref(·|q,·), Pwm via πref(·|wr,·)) are justified theoretically but not empirically tested for quality
Severe hyperparameter sensitivity (Figure 5) with scheme/model-specific tuning required (Table 7); raises fundamental concerns about generalization across new watermarks
Unclear semantic preservation metric: P-SP threshold of 0.7 appears arbitrary; divergence between Removal Rate and ESR (e.g., SIRA 88% removal but 0.5% ESR) suggests semantic metric may be weak

Incomplete understanding of watermark failures: paper demonstrates vulnerabilities but doesn't explain fundamental causes (fragile statistical signals? predictable distribution shifts? adversarial embedding patterns?)

Artificial threat model: assumes adversary has generator but not detector access; with generator access, logit-based watermarks leak greenlist information through generation patterns—unclear why RL is needed
Limited generalization validation: all models are Qwen/LLaMA from 2024; no cross-architecture evaluation or testing on older models/architectures
Key gap between instance-level threat model (r*(X)) and distribution-level approximation (r_KL): relaxation may lose important problem structure; no analysis of approximation quality

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across 10 watermarking schemes, 5 model sizes, and multiple text lengths with strong experimental documentation
Well-motivated theoretical framework (adaptive robustness radius) that provides principled perspective on watermark security, with formal Theorem 1 guaranteeing KL-constrained robustness
Important practical insights: system prompts significantly boost attacks (understudied in prior work), reasoning capability degrades watermark resilience, long-form robustness is weaker than claimed
Striking empirical results: 98.5% ESR with only 100 training samples and zero detector access substantially exceeds prior work (GPT-4o: 6.75%)
Extensive reproducibility support with detailed hyperparameters, implementation details, and thorough ablations (OOD generalization, mixed-key training, training set size sensitivity)
Detection score distribution analysis (Figure 4b) demonstrates RLCracker aligns paraphrased outputs with unwatermarked distributions, not just erasing watermarks
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: Adaptive robustness radius (Theorem 1) provides bounds on expected scores but the practical RL objective (Eq. 1) doesn't explicitly optimize this radius; connection between minimizing theoretical objective and empirical success is indirect
Assumption 1 (sub-Gaussian detector score) is strong and unvalidated empirically for complex schemes like SIR/X-SIR; violation of this assumption invalidates theoretical guarantees

Critical hyperparameter sensitivity: RLCracker requires different weight configurations (w₁, w₂, w₃) per watermarking scheme (Table 7) and is highly sensitive (Figure 5), but paper doesn't address how attackers determine optimal weights without detector access, undermining 'detector-free' claims
Reference model choice for Ph (using base model πref) is somewhat circular and lacks rigorous justification; unclear why base model adequately proxies human-like text
P-SP semantic similarity threshold (0.7) is arbitrary with no sensitivity analysis; median P-SP ranges 0.75-0.95 across conditions, so threshold changes could materially affect conclusions

Training data accessibility understudied: 100 watermarked samples requires either repeated generator queries or detector access/side information; practical feasibility in real-world settings is unclear
Limited algorithmic novelty: RLCracker uses standard GRPO with semantic+KL rewards; the main contribution is empirical evaluation rather than methodological innovation

Unigram watermark shows lower ESR (67-98.5%) than other schemes but paper provides no analysis of why RLCracker struggles with certain watermark properties or what design characteristics make attacks harder
No direct comparison with concurrent work B⁴ across full set of watermarks; limited to single model in Table 1
Ethical concerns underexplored: no mention of responsible disclosure to watermark developers, no discussion of coordinated disclosure timeline, no analysis of misuse prevention

strengths: Novel theoretical framework: The adaptive robustness radius provides a principled way to evaluate worst-case watermark resilience, grounded in certified robustness literature. Theorem 4.3 is technically sound with proper proofs.

Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Thorough testing across 10 watermarking schemes, 5 model scales, and multiple text lengths (250-1500 tokens), with extensive ablation studies and supplementary analyses (40+ page appendix).

Practical effectiveness: RLCracker achieves 98.5% removal success on challenging 1500-token texts with only 100 training samples, substantially outperforming GPT-4o and other baselines while maintaining semantic fidelity.
Strong generalization: Demonstrates effectiveness across diverse watermarking families (logit-based and sampling-based) and shows good OOD generalization to different model generators (Tables 8-9).
Well-motivated problem: Addresses real limitations in prior watermark robustness evaluations by introducing worst-case rather than average-case analysis with adaptive adversaries.
weaknesses: Substantial theory-practice gap: The theoretical framework defines r*(X) as a worst-case metric, but RLCracker doesn't directly optimize this objective. The connection between the RL algorithm's objective (max KL divergence) and the certified radius is validated empirically (Appendix D.9) but lacks theoretical guarantees. The approximation quality of the KL relaxation has no formal error bounds.

Approximation not validated: The practical instantiation of P_h and P_wm via reference model with simple prompts is a significant approximation not covered by theory. No validation that these distributions actually approximate 'human-like' and 'watermark-induced' behavior across schemes.

Limited algorithmic novelty: RLCracker is primarily GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) with token-wise KL rewards. While effective, the approach is largely engineering-focused with limited conceptual novelty compared to prior RL-based attacks.
Poor cross-watermark transfer: Models trained on one scheme fail to generalize to others (Table 20), with 13-58% ESR drops. This severely limits practical applicability of a single trained model.

Hyperparameter sensitivity and reproducibility: Extreme dependence on weights (w1, w2, w3) with 10-20x variations across schemes (Table 6). Figure 5 shows sharp ESR degradation outside optimal ranges, raising reproducibility concerns despite hyperparameter tables provided.

strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 model sizes, 10 watermarking schemes, 4 datasets, and 2 text lengths with detailed ablations
Data-efficient attack requiring only 100 training samples versus 100k for prior work (B4), representing practical improvement
High-quality results maintaining semantic preservation (P-SP > 0.7) while achieving watermark removal, with clear ESR metric distinguishing removal from preservation
Interesting empirical findings about system prompts and reasoning capabilities improving attack success
Honest discussion of limitations and thoughtful impact statement with recommendations for responsible deployment
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice disconnect: theoretical framework assumes access to true distributions P_wm and P_h, but practical algorithm approximates these via single reference model forward passes without rigorous validation
Limited theoretical novelty: Theorem 4.3 is standard application of Donsker-Varadhan inequality and sub-Gaussian concentration rather than novel contribution

Poor cross-watermark transferability undermines broad effectiveness claims: model trained on EWD achieves 93% ESR on EWD but only 13% on Unigram and 37% on PF, meaning defenders can easily deploy multiple schemes
Core finding (watermarks vulnerable to paraphrasing with proper prompting) replicates prior work (SIRA, DPO, Krishna et al.); novelty is primarily the RL implementation
Unfair experimental comparisons: ESR metric inherently penalizes methods like SIRA that trade semantic preservation for removal, making comparison with lower P-SP scores misleading

Arbitrary design choices insufficiently justified: P-SP threshold of 0.7, semantic reward sigmoid threshold of 0.85, specific hyperparameter weights per scheme (Table 6) suggesting method requires careful tuning despite efficiency claims
Reference model dependency unexplored: Appendix D.10 shows Qwen3-8B vs Qwen3-0.6B as P_wm proxy produces very different results (57% vs 91.5% ESR), indicating high sensitivity
No defense mechanisms proposed, limiting impact of identifying vulnerabilities; paper is purely attack-oriented

Threat model assumptions partially unrealistic: requiring 100 watermarked examples is still substantial knowledge of watermarking system; computational cost (1.5 hours on 4 A100s) not discussed or contextualized

strengths: Novel theoretical framework (adaptive robustness radius) bridging certified robustness to watermarking, with practical KL-divergence approximation and formal lower bound (Theorem 4.3)
Impressive practical efficiency: achieves 98.5% watermark removal with only 100 training samples, zero detector access, and minimal computational requirements (0.5-1.5 hours)

Exceptionally comprehensive experimental evaluation: 10 watermarking schemes, 5 model sizes, multiple text lengths with thorough ablations on training data, mixed-key robustness, and cross-model transfer
Valuable practical insights about overlooked vulnerabilities: system prompts, reasoning capabilities, and test-time scaling that are actionable for watermark designers
Strong reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, standard toolkit usage, clear experimental protocols, and promised code release
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: adaptive robustness radius nominally requires detector access yet threat model claims zero access; KL radius is a lower bound on an already-relaxed notion, making tightness guarantees unclear

Poor cross-watermark transferability undermines claimed broad effectiveness: training on one watermark (EWD) achieves only 13.3% ESR on Unigram vs. 67% Base, limiting applicability when watermark type unknown
Limited defensive guidance: paper excels at attack but provides minimal analysis of watermark design principles that confer robustness or recommendations beyond increasing embedding strength

Reference distribution approximation concerns: P_h approximated via model rather than human text; Table 13 shows high sensitivity to proxy choice (91.5% → 57% ESR), and Appendix D.16 validation shows persistent distribution gaps

Semantic similarity metric limitations: P-SP score is relatively simple without human evaluation validation; threshold (0.7) appears arbitrary with high sensitivity shown in Figure 7; some outputs show fluency degradation (PPL 2.83 on XSIR vs. 3.11 baseline)
